questions.q: Which of these does NOT trigger a rebalance of a consumer group subscribed to topic `orders`?

options.t: A new consumer joins the group
options.why: Members joining or leaving trigger a rebalance.

options.t: A consumer stops heartbeating for longer than the session timeout
options.why: Failure detection removes the member and rebalances.

options.t: A producer starts writing to `orders` with a new key
Partitions are added to `orders`
options.why: New partitions in a subscribed topic trigger a rebalance.

questions.explain: Rebalances follow changes to the group or to what it reads: members joining or leaving, failure detection, new partitions in a subscribed topic, or a new topic matching a subscribed pattern. A new key in the data changes none of these.

questions.q: A consumer keeps heartbeating, but one batch of records takes 7 minutes to process before the next `poll()`. Settings are default. What happens?

options.t: Nothing, because heartbeats keep it in the group
options.why: Heartbeats prove the process is alive, but max.poll.interval.ms separately requires progress.

options.t: It is removed from the group after 5 minutes and its partitions are reassigned
The broker extends the poll interval automatically
options.why: There is no automatic extension; the interval is a client setting.

options.t: The records are redelivered to the same consumer after the 45 s session timeout
options.why: Redelivery to another member follows the rebalance, not a 45 s timer.

questions.explain: A consumer that heartbeats but doesn't call `poll` within `max.poll.interval.ms` (default 300 000 ms) is considered failed and the group rebalances. A later `commitSync` fails with `CommitFailedException`.

questions.q: A team deploys a consumer application by restarting its instances one by one, and each restart causes two rebalances. Which setting is designed to stop restarts from triggering rebalances?

options.t: group.instance.id, with a long enough session timeout
enable.auto.commit=false, so restarts don't commit partway through a batch
options.why: Commit style doesn't affect when rebalances happen.

options.t: auto.offset.reset=earliest
options.why: This only matters when a group has no committed offset.

options.t: max.poll.records=1
options.why: This changes batch size, not membership.

questions.explain: Static membership gives each instance a persistent id, so a restart within the session timeout rejoins as the same member without a rebalance.

questions.q: In Kafka 4.x, a team wants its consumers to use the newer consumer group protocol (KIP-848). What must they do on the client?

options.t: Nothing; Kafka 4.x clients use it by default
options.why: It is enabled on the server by default, but not on the client.

options.t: Set partition.assignment.strategy=uniform
options.why: Assignment moves to the broker under the new protocol; this client setting is for the classic protocol.

options.t: Set session.timeout.ms on each consumer
options.why: Under the new protocol the session timeout is set on the broker, and the client setting can't be used.

options.t: Set group.protocol=consumer

questions.explain: The new protocol is on by default on 4.x brokers but not on clients: a consumer opts in with `group.protocol=consumer`. Heartbeat, session timeout and assignment are then set on the broker.

questions.q: A consumer commits its offset right after `poll()` returns, then processes the records. It crashes halfway through a batch. What delivery semantics does this give?

options.t: At least once: the batch is reprocessed on restart
options.why: The offset was already committed past the batch, so it is not read again.

options.t: At most once: the rest of the batch is never processed
Exactly once, because the commit is synchronous and happens first
options.why: Synchronous commits don't make processing exactly-once.

options.t: It depends only on the producer's acks
options.why: acks affects writes; this is about when the consumer saves its position.

questions.explain: Saving the position before processing gives at-most-once on a crash. Processing first, then saving, gives at-least-once.

questions.q: Which delivery semantics does Kafka give by default?

options.t: At most once
options.why: That requires turning retries off and committing before processing.

options.t: Exactly once end to end
options.why: That needs transactions and read_committed (or Kafka Streams with exactly_once_v2).

options.t: At least once
None; delivery is best effort
options.why: Kafka documents at-least-once as its default.

questions.explain: The design docs state that Kafka guarantees at-least-once delivery by default.

questions.q: A Kafka-to-Kafka application reads from one topic, transforms each record, and writes to another. Which are needed for exactly-once processing with the plain clients?

options.t: A transactional producer that sends the consumer's offsets in the same transaction as the output
acks=1 on the producer
options.why: Transactions require idempotence, which requires acks=all.

options.t: enable.auto.commit=true on the consumer
options.why: Offsets must be committed through the transaction, so auto-commit is off.

options.t: Downstream consumers using isolation.level=read_committed
A replication factor equal to the number of consumers
options.why: Replication factor is unrelated to exactly-once processing.

questions.explain: Exactly-once Kafka to Kafka: the transactional producer writes output and offsets atomically, and readers use `read_committed` so aborted output is hidden.

questions.q: How does the idempotent producer prevent duplicates caused by its own retries?

options.t: The broker deduplicates using a producer ID and sequence numbers
The producer waits for a consumer to confirm before sending the next record
options.why: Producers never wait for consumers.

options.t: The broker compares each record's value with the last 1000 records
options.why: Deduplication uses producer ID and sequence numbers, not content.

options.t: It disables retries, so nothing is ever sent twice
options.why: Idempotence requires retries > 0.

questions.explain: The broker assigns each producer an ID and uses the sequence number on each message to discard duplicates from retries.

questions.q: In Kafka 4.3, a developer creates a producer and sets only bootstrap.servers and the two serializers. Is it idempotent?

options.t: No; enable.idempotence must be set to true explicitly
options.why: It has been on by default since Kafka 3.0.

options.t: Only if transactional.id is set
options.why: transactional.id implies idempotence, but idempotence is on without it.

options.t: No, because the default acks is 1
options.why: The default acks is all.

options.t: Yes; it is on by default unless settings conflict

questions.explain: `enable.idempotence` defaults to true, with `acks=all` the default too. It is silently turned off only if conflicting settings are set and idempotence was not explicitly enabled.

questions.q: Where are consumer group offsets stored, and what replication does that topic get by default?

options.t: In ZooKeeper, with no replication
options.why: Offsets moved into Kafka long ago, and 4.x has no ZooKeeper.

options.t: In __consumer_offsets, replication factor 3 by default
On each consumer's local disk
options.why: The committed position is stored by Kafka so a restarted consumer can recover it.

options.t: In __cluster_metadata, the KRaft metadata log, with replication factor 1
options.why: That is the KRaft metadata log, not group offsets.

questions.explain: Committed offsets go to the internal offsets topic, with `offsets.topic.replication.factor` 3 and `offsets.topic.num.partitions` 50 by default.

questions.q: A consumer group was shut down for a 10-day maintenance freeze. When it restarts, it starts from auto.offset.reset instead of where it stopped. Why?

options.t: Committed offsets expired 7 days after the group became empty
The topic's retention.ms deleted the offsets along with the old data
options.why: Offset expiry is a broker setting on the offsets, separate from the topic's data retention.

options.t: Offsets are kept only while the producer is running
options.why: Offsets belong to the consumer group, not the producer.

options.t: The group protocol changed during the freeze
options.why: The protocol doesn't erase committed offsets.

questions.explain: `offsets.retention.minutes` defaults to 10 080 (7 days): committed offsets expire that long after a group becomes empty, after which `auto.offset.reset` applies.

questions.q: How do share groups ("queues for Kafka") differ from consumer groups?

options.t: Share groups replace consumer groups in Kafka 4.x
options.why: They are a different kind of group alongside consumer groups.

options.t: Share groups store records in a separate queue log
options.why: They read ordinary topic partitions.

options.t: Several consumers can share a partition, acknowledging records one by one
Share groups guarantee per-key ordering across all consumers of a partition
options.why: Cooperative consumption of one partition by many consumers trades away that ordering.

questions.explain: Share consumers cooperatively consume: a partition can be assigned to several consumers, consumers can outnumber partitions, and records are acknowledged individually with counted delivery attempts.

questions.q: What replication factor does the Apache Kafka documentation recommend so machines can be bounced without interrupting consumption?

options.why: One replica means the data is unavailable while its broker is down.

options.t: 2 or 3
Equal to the number of partitions
options.why: Replication factor and partition count are unrelated.

options.t: At least 7
options.why: The docs recommend 2 or 3.

questions.explain: The docs recommend a replication factor of 2 or 3; with 3, up to 2 servers can fail before you lose access to the data.

questions.q: A producer writes to a topic that doesn't exist, on a cluster with default broker settings. What happens?

options.t: The write fails with InvalidTopicException
options.why: That is for invalid names; a missing topic is created by default.

options.t: The record is held until an administrator creates the topic
options.why: Topics are created on first use by default.

options.t: The record goes to a default topic
options.why: There is no default topic.

options.t: It is created with 1 partition and replication factor 1

questions.explain: `auto.create.topics.enable` is true by default, and new topics get `num.partitions=1` and `default.replication.factor=1`, which is rarely what production wants.

questions.q: Why does `kafka-topics --create` warn when a topic name contains a period or an underscore?

options.t: Names like orders.eu and orders_eu can collide in metric names
Periods and underscores are not allowed in topic names
options.why: They are allowed; the tool only warns.

options.t: They make the topic compacted by default
options.why: Names don't affect the cleanup policy.

options.t: They limit the topic to one partition
options.why: Names don't affect partition count.

questions.explain: Topic names may use ASCII letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, but because of metric naming, topics with a period or underscore could collide, so the tool warns.

questions.q: A broker that leads several partitions fails. Who chooses the new leaders, and from where?

options.t: The producers vote, choosing the replica with the most data
options.why: Clients don't elect leaders.

options.t: The consumers' group coordinator, from any replica
options.why: The group coordinator handles groups, not partitions.

options.t: The controller, from the in-sync replicas
Each remaining broker promotes itself
options.why: Elections are made by the controller, not by brokers themselves.

questions.explain: On broker failure the controller elects new leaders from the ISR, batching the changes across partitions.

questions.q: A broker is stopped with a controlled shutdown (the default). What does it do before stopping?

options.t: It deletes its local partitions so the controller can reassign them elsewhere
options.why: Data stays on disk; only leadership moves.

options.t: It moves leadership of its partitions to other replicas first
Waits for every consumer group to commit
options.why: Shutdown doesn't wait for consumers.

options.t: Copies its data to a new broker
options.why: Reassignment is a separate, manual tool.

questions.explain: With `controlled.shutdown.enable` (default true) the broker syncs its logs and moves leadership of its partitions to other replicas before stopping, cutting unavailability to a few milliseconds when each partition has another live replica.

questions.q: Kafka keeps high throughput while writing every record to disk. Which design choices does the documentation give for this?

options.t: It relies on the operating system's page cache and sequential writes
It keeps each topic fully in the JVM heap
options.why: Kafka deliberately avoids an in-process cache.

options.t: Batches stay compressed in the log and are decompressed by the consumer
It writes every record with fsync before acknowledging
options.why: Kafka relies on replication rather than fsync on every write.

options.t: It stores each record in its own file
options.why: Records are appended to segment files.

questions.explain: The design relies on the OS page cache and linear writes rather than an in-process cache, and on end-to-end batch compression: compressed batches stay compressed in the log.

questions.q: Which statement about tiered storage in Apache Kafka 4.3 is true?

options.t: It is enabled by default, and Kafka ships an S3 RemoteStorageManager to use
options.why: It is off by default, and Kafka ships no RemoteStorageManager implementation.

options.t: It works with compacted topics
options.why: The docs list compacted topics as not supported.

options.t: It moves active segments to remote storage as they are written
options.why: Only completed segments are moved.

options.t: It offloads completed segments; you must plug in a RemoteStorageManager

questions.explain: Tiered storage keeps completed log segments in a remote tier; it is off by default, has no built-in `RemoteStorageManager`, and doesn't support compacted topics.

questions.q: What does the LAG column in `kafka-consumer-groups --describe` show for a partition?

options.t: The difference between the log-end offset and the group's current (committed) offset
The time since the last record was produced
options.why: Lag here is a count of records, not time.

options.t: The number of replicas out of sync
options.why: That is under-replication, a broker metric.

options.t: The number of records the producer has buffered
options.why: The group tool reads the log and the group's offsets, not producer buffers.

questions.explain: `--describe` shows CURRENT-OFFSET, LOG-END-OFFSET and LAG for each partition: how far the group is behind the end of the log.

questions.q: A team wants to replay the last 24 hours of `orders` for group `billing`. Which conditions must hold for `kafka-consumer-groups --reset-offsets --to-datetime ... --execute` to work?

options.t: The billing group's consumers must be inactive
The topic must be compacted
options.why: Resetting offsets works on any topic.

options.t: The command must name --topic (or --all-topics)
The producer must be paused
options.why: Producers are unaffected by a group's offsets.

options.t: The command must be run on the partition leader's host
options.why: It connects with --bootstrap-server from anywhere.

questions.explain: `--reset-offsets` works on one group at a time, needs `--topic` or `--all-topics`, requires the group's consumers to be inactive, and only shows the plan unless `--execute` is given.

questions.q: What are the three capabilities the Apache Kafka documentation says Kafka combines for event streaming?

options.t: Batch ETL, data warehousing and reporting
options.why: Those describe batch analytics, not event streaming.

options.t: Request/response messaging, caching and load balancing across services
options.why: Kafka is not a request/response system.

options.t: Publish/subscribe, durable storage, and stream processing
Encryption, compression and replication only
options.why: These are features, not the three capabilities the docs describe.

questions.explain: Kafka combines publish/subscribe (including import and export), durable storage, and processing of streams of events as they occur or retrospectively.

questions.q: A producer sends records with no key and no partition specified, using the default partitioner. How are they spread?

options.t: Strict round-robin: one record to each partition in turn, then repeat
options.why: The default is sticky, not per-record round-robin.

options.t: All to partition 0
options.why: Records are spread; partition 0 is not special.

options.t: By a hash of the value
options.why: Only the key is hashed; values never choose the partition.

options.t: To a sticky partition that changes after a batch fills

questions.explain: With no key, the default logic sends to a sticky partition that changes after at least `batch.size` bytes have gone to it, which keeps batches large.
